source: Christianson, Hollingworth, Halliwell, Ferreira (2001) Thematic roles assigned along the garden path linger
finding: Five experiments on garden-path sentences like 'While the man hunted the deer ran into the woods'. After reading, many people still say the man hunted the deer, even though the sentence says he did not. Reanalysis is partial: the old role stays while the new one is built. Authors conclude the goal of processing is a representation that is 'good enough'.
numbers: Exp 1a: 36 students, 134 sentences. Incorrect 'yes' to 'did the man hunt the deer': long ambiguous region 47.4% vs short 32.1%; plausible 47.6% vs implausible 32.0%; plausible garden path 47.6% vs control 26.2%. Exp 2: matrix-clause questions answered correctly about 90% of the time.
quote: the goal of language processing is not always to create an idealized structure, but rather to create a representation that is 'good enough'
limits: Undergraduates, written sentences, yes/no probes. Later critics said the probe question could re-create the misparse (answered by Patson et al. 2009).
agent_relevance: S1: a fluent, internally consistent reading can still hold a wrong sub-claim. The agent should probe each stated sub-claim separately rather than trust one global read.

source: Christianson et al. (2001) Exp 2 and 3: question type and clause order
finding: The same sentence gave mostly correct answers to the question about the new structure (matrix clause) but many errors to the question about the old structure (subordinate clause). Both propositions were held at once, which a clean full reanalysis would not allow.
numbers: Exp 2 style contrast: incorrect 'yes' 55.6% for subordinate-clause questions vs 9.4% for matrix-clause questions (F1(1,23)=70.08). Another condition: 36.1% garden path vs 13.5% control (F1(1,35)=36.63).
limits: Percentages taken from the results text; exact table-to-condition mapping is in the paper.
agent_relevance: Yes answers to two probes summing to more than 100% is the signature to look for: two incompatible readings stored together. A consistency check across paired probes can detect it in a model.

source: Christianson et al. (2001) Exps 3a/3b: syntactically unusual verbs, against general reasoning
finding: Used verbs of a small class (reflexive absolute transitive, RAT) to test if the misreading is just pragmatic inference. Misinterpretation was lower for RAT verbs, but clause order still mattered, so it is a parsing effect, not only world-knowledge inference.
numbers: Exp 3: incorrect 'yes' 62.0% (optionally transitive verbs) vs 39.1% (RAT verbs), F1(1,15)=35.61; subordinate-matrix order 70.3% vs matrix-subordinate 30.7%.
limits: Small verb set; 16 participants in this analysis.
agent_relevance: Surface form changes error rates even when meaning is the same. Test the agent on reordered, meaning-equal restatements of a prompt.

source: Patson et al. (2009) Lingering misinterpretations in garden-path sentences: evidence from a paraphrasing task
finding: Replicates Christianson 2001 without any yes/no probe. People paraphrase garden-path sentences in a way that keeps the old reading, so the effect is not caused by the question.
numbers: 50 participants, 96 sentences. Partial-reanalysis paraphrases: ambiguous 72% vs disambiguated (comma) 29% (F1(1,49)=140.98). Full reanalysis: 21% ambiguous vs 62% disambiguated. Nearly 70% of paraphrases in the ambiguous case showed partial reanalysis. 'Other' 4% of data. In the original probe task, about 60% said yes to the misreading and nearly 90% yes to the correct reading.
limits: Paraphrases coded by hand into four categories. Kaschak and Glenberg (2004) argued for memory traces rather than partial reanalysis; not ruled out here.
agent_relevance: A free-form restatement test is a cleaner way to see what the agent understood than a leading yes/no check, and avoids reinstating the wrong reading.

source: Ferreira and Patson (2007) The 'Good Enough' approach to language comprehension
finding: Reviews the theory: comprehension builds a representation only as detailed as the task needs, using heuristics (first noun is the agent) alongside full syntax. Covers Moses illusion, bury-the-survivors, passives, garden paths, local coherence, disfluency repairs.
numbers: Passives: a large proportion of students named the wrong agent (no exact number in this review). Ungrammatical 'While Katie fixed the car hit a fire hydrant' judged grammatical on about one third of trials, much more than ordinary ungrammatical items.
quote: people's comprehension of sentences can be quite shallow
limits: A review; exact figures are in the cited originals. Authors stress that most of the time the result is right or harmless.
agent_relevance: S1: the agent must decide what 'correct' needs: the task's real question, not the surface of the text. Depth must be forced when the task needs it.

source: Ferreira (2003) passives and clefts, as reported in Ferreira and Patson (2007)
finding: Unambiguous passives such as 'the dog was bitten by the man' often get the wrong agent. 'It was the man who bit the dog' is understood well though rarer, so frequency does not explain it. A first-noun-is-agent heuristic (Bever 1970) does.
numbers: A 'large proportion' of wrong agent answers; cleft form understood perfectly. Exact percentages not read this session.
limits: Second-hand: read only via the 2007 review.
agent_relevance: Heuristic readings beat syntax even with ample time. An agent should re-derive roles on non-canonical sentences when roles decide the answer.

source: Erickson and Mattson (1981) From words to meanings: a semantic illusion, as reported in Ferreira and Patson (2007)
finding: The Moses illusion: asked 'How many of each type of animal did Moses take on the ark?', most people say 'two' and miss that it was Noah. Partial matching in semantic memory is enough to pass.
numbers: Original percentages not read; the review says most people respond two. It also cites Barton and Sanford 1993 'bury the survivors'.
limits: Second-hand. Later work shows detection depends on semantic closeness of the swapped word (see a21).
agent_relevance: A false presupposition inside a question is a direct S1 trap: the answer can be fluent and look correct while answering the wrong question.

source: Frances (2024) Good enough processing: what have we learned in the 20 years since Ferreira et al. (2002)?
finding: Reviews the roughly 20 studies, out of 500+ citing papers, that directly test the three claims: ambiguity stays unresolved, heuristics are used, depth depends on task. Evidence is mixed. Main criticism: it is a guiding principle, too vague to be falsified, because deeper processing can always be said to be task-required.
numbers: 11 studies on claim 1, 8 on claim 3, about 20 direct tests overall. Logacev and Vasishth 2016: partial-specification models affected answers on 17% of trials; non-specification models fit better.
quote: good enough processing is too vague to be falsifiable
limits: One author's synthesis; categories chosen by the reviewer.
agent_relevance: Use the idea as a design principle, not a law: a rule 'shallow unless the task needs depth' needs an explicit trigger, or it cannot be checked.

source: Swets et al. (2008) and Tan and Foltz (2020) underspecification of syntactic ambiguity, as reviewed in Frances (2024)
finding: Ambiguous relative-clause attachment ('the maid of the princess who scratched herself') is read faster than disambiguated versions, but only when people expect shallow questions. With deep questions the advantage disappears: depth follows task.
numbers: Ambiguity advantage in self-paced reading only under superficial-question expectation. Tan and Foltz found the same in Chinese learners of English.
limits: Second-hand via review.
agent_relevance: Direct support for task-dependent depth: telling the agent what kind of check follows changes how carefully it reads. The reverse is the risk.

source: Slattery et al. (2013) as reviewed in Frances (2024)
finding: Eye tracking shows a proper structure is built on first reading (reflexive gender-mismatch effects appear), yet the misparse lingers into the next sentence when the wrong reading is plausible. Offline errors come from leftovers, not from never reanalysing.
numbers: Exp 2: slowdown in the next sentence only when the garden path was plausible (truck vs grass). Exact ms not read.
limits: Second-hand via review.
agent_relevance: Plausibility of the wrong reading, not syntax, predicts the error. An agent is most at risk when the wrong answer is believable.

source: Qian et al. (2018), Chromy (2022), Nakamura and Arai (2016) as reviewed in Frances (2024): competing explanations
finding: Qian: P600 reanalysis effort did not differ for correct and incorrect answers, against lazy reanalysis, yet likelihood of the wrong reading predicted accuracy (pro-heuristic). Chromy: garden paths raise errors on unrelated misreadings too, so they may simply be hard. Nakamura and Arai: misanalysis persists even when pragmatics cannot support it.
numbers: No effect sizes read this session.
limits: Second-hand. The lingering-misinterpretation effect has at least three accounts: partial reanalysis, memory traces, plain difficulty.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one mechanism for a model's errors either; keep failure analysis open.

source: Sanford et al. (2011) and Sturt et al. (2004) as reviewed in Frances (2024)
finding: Easy-to-detect anomalies give an N400; hard ones (fit the context) give only a late positivity near 800 ms. In change detection, an unfocused word swapped to a related word is hardest to notice. Not every part of a sentence is processed to the same depth.
numbers: No percentages read.
limits: Second-hand via review.
agent_relevance: Detail is lost where text fits expectations and is not emphasised. Mark the load-bearing words of a prompt explicitly.

source: Frank and Goodman (2012) Predicting pragmatic reasoning in language games (Rational Speech Act model)
finding: A listener picks a referent by Bayes: posterior is proportional to how likely an informative speaker would use that word for the object, times object salience. Informativeness is information-theoretic (a word that fits fewer objects is more informative). No free parameters.
numbers: Three groups bet on objects. Speaker condition vs model r = .98; salience vs listener r = .19 (n.s.); model combining informativeness and salience vs listener r = .99 (r = .87 with 0 and 100 predictions removed). Listener N = 263, speaker N = 206, salience prior N = 20; supplement reports 745 participants in total.
limits: Tiny reference game with few objects and one-word utterances. Does not model irony, indirect requests or long text.
agent_relevance: The cleanest formal model of inferring what is meant. An agent can use it as a check: of the things the asker could have said, why did they say this one?

source: Grice (1975) Logic and conversation: cooperative principle and maxims
finding: Speakers follow quantity, quality, relation and manner. Listeners derive implicatures from apparent violations. The base for modern pragmatics and for implicature tests of LLMs.
numbers: Not quantitative.
limits: Not opened this session; stated from background knowledge. URL is a general reference.
agent_relevance: A prompt is a cooperative utterance: unusual wording or an included detail is a signal. The agent should ask what the detail is for.

source: Ruis et al. (2022) The Goldilocks of pragmatic understanding: fine-tuning strategy matters for implicature resolution by LLMs
finding: Tested LLMs on yes/no implicature resolution ('Did you leave fingerprints?' 'I wore gloves' means no). Base models, dialogue-tuned models and benchmark-level instruction-tuned models were close to chance. Models instruction-tuned at the example level did much better.
numbers: Humans 86.2% average (best human 92%). Pretrained models about 60% zero-shot. 600 test items. GPT-4 82.3% +/- 1.4 (3.9 points below humans); Cohere-command-52B 72.8%; text-davinci-003 60.2% at k=0 to 75.4%; ChatGPT 75.1%. Base models best 68.7% (GPT-3-175b, k=5); BlenderBot 47.0% at k=5.
limits: Binary yes/no format. Models from 2022-2023.
agent_relevance: Pragmatic skill came from training on task-style examples, not from scale alone. A scaffold cannot rely on a base model to infer implied answers.

source: Ruis et al. (2022): context-heavy versus context-free implicature
finding: Particularised implicatures (need context: 'Want to stay for a nightcap?' 'I've gotta get up early' means no) are harder than generalised ones ('Some' means not all) for humans and models. Chain-of-thought closes most of the gap for GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-4 30-shot: 71.97% on particularised vs humans 83.18%; GPT-4 5-shot CoT 81.63%. Generalised: GPT-4 30-shot 86.23%, with CoT 88.66%. 217 of 600 test items hand-labelled by type.
limits: Only 217 of 600 labelled.
agent_relevance: Spelling out the context step by step helps most on cases that depend on context. Use an explicit 'what must the speaker believe' step for implied answers.

source: Ruis et al. (2022): few-shot examples teach the answer format, not pragmatics
finding: Random-label few-shot examples did not hurt Cohere-command-52B or text-davinci-001, so shots mostly fix the yes/no output format. Cohere jumped from k=0 to k=1 because of calibration, not understanding.
numbers: Cohere-command-52B: sharp rise from 0 to 1 shot; random labels did not degrade results. Benchmark-level instruction-tuned models got worse for k>0.
limits: Tested in Appendix K.6 on two models only.
agent_relevance: Do not count a gain from examples as a gain in understanding. Test with shuffled labels.

source: Hu, Floyd, Jouravlev, Fedorenko, Gibson (2023) A fine-grained comparison of pragmatic language understanding in humans and language models
finding: Seven pragmatic tasks (deceits, indirect speech, irony, maxims, metaphor, humor, coherence), multiple choice with typed distractors. Largest models were above chance on all tasks and near humans on some. Within errors they favour the literal option over heuristic distractors, like humans.
numbers: Models: GPT-2, Flan-T5 base/XL, Tk-Instruct 3B/11B, InstructGPT-3 ada, text-davinci-002. Smallest three at chance. Worst tasks: humor, irony, maxims. text-davinci-002 picked the human-preferred punchline only 55% of the time. Humans mostly pick Correct, sometimes Literal, rarely distractors.
limits: Older models; items from Floyd et al. (in prep).
agent_relevance: Failure type matters: a literal reading is the typical model error. Check for a literal answer to a non-literal request.

source: Hu et al. (2023): context ablation and item-level agreement
finding: Scrambling or removing context lowered accuracy for models; by-item model probability was compared with human accuracy. Suggests similar cue use without explicit mind modelling.
numbers: Exact correlations are in the paper's figures; not transcribed here.
limits: Preliminary evidence; human scrambling not run in every condition.
agent_relevance: Surface cues can support pragmatic answers, which also means they can mislead.

source: Dentella, Gunther, Murphy, Marcus, Leivada (2023/2024) Testing AI on language comprehension tasks reveals insensitivity to underlying meaning
finding: Seven LLMs answered comprehension questions on short texts with common constructions, each prompted several times. As a group they were at chance and unstable across repeats; 400 humans did better with different error types.
numbers: n = 26,680 datapoints. Group accuracy at chance; Mixtral first to perform at chance; Llama2 mean accuracy .66 first above chance; only Falcon, Llama2 and ChatGPT-4 above chance.
limits: Authors are sceptics of LLM understanding; benchmark is theirs and not independently validated. Human accuracy figure not extracted.
agent_relevance: Answers that change on re-asking show weak grounding. Instability across repeats is a cheap warning signal for code to use.

source: Cai, Duan, Haslett, Wang, Pickering (2023/2024) Do large language models resemble humans in language use?
finding: Twelve preregistered psycholinguistic tests. ChatGPT matched humans on 10, Vicuna on 7. In the Moses-style semantic illusion test, ChatGPT but not Vicuna noticed fewer errors than baseline when the wrong word was close to the right one; both detected far fewer errors than humans.
numbers: Semantic illusion: 72 items (54 targets, 18 fillers). After removing 2 items, ChatGPT error reports: baseline 0.00 vs strong imposter 0.14 and weak imposter 0.17 (z = 12.55 and 13.27, p < .001), no difference between imposters (p = .109). Vicuna: .002 vs .022 and .018, n.s. Neither model used context to resolve syntactic ambiguity.
limits: Items modified from originals; only condition means for humans. ChatGPT version 9 Jan 2022.
agent_relevance: Models miss anomalies even more than people. Tell the agent to check premises of a question explicitly.

source: Cai et al. (2023): inference drawing
finding: Both models said 'yes' far more often to explicitly stated facts than to bridging or elaborative inferences, so inferences beyond the text were often not drawn.
numbers: ChatGPT 'yes': explicit 0.95, bridging 0.49, elaborative 0.23 (23 items). Vicuna: 0.79, 0.24, 0.20; Vicuna did not separate bridging from elaborative (p = .900).
limits: Prompt wording and answer format may drive yes rates.
agent_relevance: Models are conservative about unstated implications. For implied answers, prompt explicitly for what follows.

source: Amouyal et al. (2025) When the LM misunderstood, the human chuckled: garden path effects in humans and language models
finding: Tested three hypotheses of why garden-path sentences are hard, on humans and a suite of LLMs, with comprehension questions, paraphrase and text-to-image. LLMs also fail on garden-path sentences though they see the whole sentence at once. Plausibility has the strongest effect in humans.
numbers: Humans: 95.4% on simple questions (min 92.4, max 98.7) vs 37.0% on garden-path questions. GLMM: GP vs non-GP p = .019 (implausible) and 2.5e-13 (reflexive); plausible vs implausible p = 4.1e-16; transitivity-bias correlation r = .19. Best LLM o1-preview 78%, Gemma-27B 74%. Paraphrase: non-GP above 90% for almost all LLMs, GP lower.
limits: Each item shown to 10 human participants; English only; LLM list as of early 2025.
agent_relevance: Even strong reasoning models show a human-like lingering misreading, so a plain re-read will not catch it. Use a check from another angle (paraphrase, separate probes).

source: Amouyal et al. (2025): human and LLM item-difficulty alignment
finding: Model rank order of the six conditions matched human rank order (high Spearman) regardless of size; item-level agreement (Kendall tau) rose with size. In OLMo-7b, resemblance grows during training.
numbers: Spearman by condition high for all models; Kendall tau larger for bigger models; exact values only in figures.
limits: Rank agreement over 6 conditions is coarse.
agent_relevance: Model errors appear where human errors appear, so human findings can predict where to add checks.

source: Li et al. (2024) garden-path sentences with GPT-2, LLaMA-2, Flan-T5, RoBERTa (search summary only)
finding: Chunk-by-chunk presentation with paired questions to probe lingering misinterpretation; reported promising human-LLM alignment, strongest when extra-syntactic information guides processing.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Seen only in a search snippet; paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Same direction as Amouyal et al.; verify before using.
